chapter.title: Five Frames
chapter.sub: The anchor's voice arrives before his lips — only on the stream, only since Tuesday.

items.text: SEASON 4 · EPISODE 2 · DRAFT  Cold case · Maya, Tess and Omar · Level L3  The anchor's voice is arriving before his lips — only on the stream. Somebody changed something on Tuesday. The change log knows who.  ⚑ RV-87: sync figures simplified. RV-85: a trainee’s mistake, handled without blame. Some choices run on a clock.

items.title: Five Frames
items.stakes: Fourteen viewers say the anchor's lips are wrong. The noon news is in two hours. Someone changed something this week — and someone is going to feel terrible about it.
items.reward: Lips and voice together. Tess still on the team. Warning #6 crossed off.

objectives.text: Work out what 'stream only' rules out
Say the hard thing to Tess — the right way
Look closer: two things nobody labeled

items.rumor: The change log has a line from Tuesday afternoon. Tess hasn't looked at it. She's afraid to.

items.alt: The viewer inbox: fourteen new emails about the stream — lips wrong on the app, like a dubbed movie, the voice is early — and zero broadcast complaints. Tess and Maya read.
items.caption: Fourteen viewers. One path. Zero complaints about broadcast.

lines.text: Fourteen emails. All the stream. None about broadcast.
That's not a complaint. That's a clue.

items.alt: A living room up the valley at night. On the phone in Dolores's hand, the stream: the anchor's voice says 'valley' while his mouth is still closed.
items.caption: On the stream, the word arrives first. The lips follow a fifth of a second later.

items.title: “— Dolores, Cedar Row”
items.body: One of the fourteen. *I thought it was my eyes. Then I thought it was my ears. Then I thought, maybe it isn't me.* The same Dolores. She moved up the valley to be near Ana. She still writes to people when things are wrong — now she's sure it isn't her.

items.alt: The stream platform's automated support chat on a master-control screen: ticket received, have you tried restarting your encoder, estimated reply five to seven business days. Tess and Maya read it without expression.

bubbles.text: It says have we tried restarting.
Restarting is how you delete the only witness.

items.caption: The support bot is sympathetic the way a vending machine is sympathetic.

items.text: 🔭 PHYSICS IN MOTION  When is sound 'too early'?  The science under this episode’s problem — live.

items.sub: Intermediate · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Maya and Tess beside a board. Time equals n times one over f-p-s. n is the number of frames you measured; f-p-s is the frame rate. At twenty-nine ninety-seven. Then work it out, and that's your delay.

bubbles.text: Time equals n times one over f-p-s. n is the number of frames you measured; f-p-s is the frame rate.
Then work it out, and that's your delay.

items.caption: Intermediate: the formula and what every letter means. The arithmetic is yours.

items.text: 📗 FIELD NOTES · INTERMEDIATE  Terms   Lip sync   Frame   Formula and variables   ƒ FORMULA · Frames to time  t = n × (1 ÷ fps)   n  number of frames  fps  frames per second
Act I — “Where does the sound get ahead?”

items.alt: System View: the studio feeds two chains. The broadcast chain adds two frames to both video and audio, so it stays in sync. The stream video path adds five frames of processing; the stream audio path now has zero delay, down from 170 ms, so stream sound arrives five frames early.
items.caption: offset = audio − video. Negative means the sound is early.

items.prompt: 7:34. Two hours to the noon news. How do you find out what's really happening?
items.happening: Viewer reports: stream lips wrong. Broadcast: no complaints.
items.risk: Viewers' trust in the stream — and Tess, who doesn't know yet.
timeout: Lena asks for an update. You have opinions and no numbers.
Measurement first — or the loudest opinion decides.

hints.text: Where do viewers watch? Measure there.
A known event on both tracks: a flash and a beep.

options.label: Nudge the stream audio delay by eye on the studio monitor until it looks right
options.result: It looks right in master control. On Dolores's phone it's now two frames late.
options.consequence: You tuned it on the wrong screen.
options.fail: The studio monitor isn't where viewers watch.

options.label: Restart the stream encoder
options.result: Ninety seconds of black for stream viewers. Same offset afterwards; its session log is gone.
options.fail: A restart doesn't remove a setting — it removes the record of what happened.

options.label: Play the flash-and-beep sync clip and record the stream on a phone off the station network — then do the same for broadcast
options.result: Stream: beep five frames before the flash. Broadcast: together.
options.consequence: Stream-only, exactly five frames. The studio is cleared in four minutes.

options.label: Reply to the viewers: check your phone's settings
options.result: Omar, over your shoulder: “Fourteen people, same phone problem?”
options.consequence: Fourteen people told they're the problem.
options.fail: Blaming the viewers' devices without evidence.

items.alt: A phone held up in master control shows the sync clip recorded off the stream: the flash on frame 26, the beep on frame 21 — stream minus five frames; broadcast zero.
items.caption: Stream only. Exactly five frames. Every time.

items.title: It isn't the studio. It's five frames, exactly.
items.body: Both outputs come from the same cameras and microphones, and broadcast is perfect — so the studio is cleared. Five whole frames, steady, isn't network jitter. It's a fixed processing delay in the stream's video path that nothing is compensating any more.
items.label: Test: what does this rule out?

items.alt: In the newsroom, Omar, tie loosened, with a coffee, and Maya.

bubbles.text: I'm told my lips are wrong. Twenty years, first time.
Your lips are fine. Your voice is in a hurry. Only on the app.

lines.text: Twenty years on air. I've been called late, loud, wooden and 'a bit much.' Never early.
Your lips are fine. Your voice is in a hurry.

items.alt: Tess's cursor hovers over 'change log' on the stream chain's menu. She doesn't click.

bubbles.text: Do we have to open the change log? Logs are like test results. Once you look, it's true.
It was true before we looked. Looking is just when we find out.

items.caption: Tess clicks. Something in her face already knows.

items.label: **Learn it now:** measuring A/V sync where viewers watch.

items.alt: The stream chain's change log: Monday, a graphics preset by C.; Tuesday 14:20, stream audio delay changed from 170 ms to 0 ms by user TESS, with a note: unlabeled, looked wrong.
items.caption: Tuesday afternoon. The careful thing, done honestly — with the reason missing.

items.title: Empty since 2019
items.body: Every setting has a notes field. On the stream chain, all of them are blank except one, from years ago, in capitals: *DON'T TOUCH THE DELAYS — C.* It was in a settings export nobody opens. Cal wrote the why. He wrote it where nobody looks.

items.title: It was Tess.
items.body: The delay didn't drift and the encoder didn't glitch. On Tuesday, Tess found a 170 ms delay on the stream audio with no label and no note, decided it was a leftover mistake, and removed it. She even wrote down why. Nobody had ever written down why it was there.
items.label: Test: what's the root cause — and what does Maya do first?

items.alt: Tess sees the log line and freezes, hands up, as if she's touched something hot.

bubbles.text: That's me. I thought it was a mistake. I thought I was helping.
You were being careful with a number nobody explained.

items.prompt: It was me. Tuesday. I saw a delay with no label and I thought it was a mistake. I'll resign. I'll—

options.label: “You removed a number nobody explained. That's on the label, not on you. Help me put it back.”
options.reply: …Okay. Okay. Show me how to measure it.

options.label: “Next time ask before you change things.”

items.title: Sound printed on the picture
items.body: In 1923 the inventor Lee de Forest showed short films with sound recorded as an optical track on the film itself, beside the pictures. Because sound and image were on the same strip, they could never drift apart — the same problem studios now solve with measured delays.

items.alt: Tess's phone: a draft email to Lena, 'Dear Lena, effective immedi—', the cursor blinking. Behind her, Omar passes with a sandwich.

bubbles.text: Is that the lunch order? I'll have what the anchor's having.

items.caption: She deletes it one letter at a time. It takes longer than writing it.

items.prompt: Omar and Lena walk in as Tess stares at the log. What do you say, out loud?
items.happening: The log shows Tess removed the delay.
known: ◉ No label, no note on the setting
items.risk: A trainee's confidence — and whether anyone reports their own mistakes again.
timeout: Nobody says anything. Tess assumes the worst and drafts a resignation on her phone.
Silence after a mistake is heard as blame.

hints.text: What failed first: the person, or the missing reason?

options.label: “Tess removed an unlabeled delay. The label failed, not her. We're putting it back — measured — and writing down why.”
options.result: Lena nods. Omar: “Happens to the best. I once unplugged a prompter mid-sentence.”
options.consequence: The system gets fixed; the person stays.

options.label: “Tess changed a setting without approval.”
options.result: Tess goes red. Lena writes something down.
options.consequence: True, and useless: approval for what, against what record?
options.fail: The change was reasonable given what anyone could see. Blaming her teaches everyone to hide changes.

options.label: “Let's keep this between us and just fix it.”
options.consequence: The label problem stays invisible; the next careful person does it again.
options.fail: Hiding the cause guarantees a repeat.

options.label: “Probably a glitch. We'll see.”
options.result: Tess knows it isn't. So does Omar.
options.fail: The log says otherwise; people can read.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #33 · AVERY'S LENS  Label the why, not just the what  A setting without its reason looks like a mistake to the next careful person.  “170 ms” on the stream audio bus had no reason attached. Tess did the careful thing — and removed it.

items.alt: System View after the fix: the stream audio path now carries a 167 ms delay matching the stream video's five frames of processing, so the offset is zero on both outputs.
items.caption: Compensate by a measurement, not by a feeling.

items.label: **Fix it:** put the five frames back — by the number.

items.alt: The phone off the network again: flash and beep on the same frame. Tess points; Maya smiles.
items.caption: Proof where Dolores watches.

items.alt: Tess holds up a freshly printed label: 167 ms equals stream video processing; ask before removing — T.
items.caption: The first label Tess has ever printed. It explains a number instead of hiding it.

lines.text: It's your label maker. Can I really—
Ray gave it to me after a very bad Sunday. Now it's your very bad Tuesday.
(She prints: 167 ms = STREAM VIDEO PROCESSING. ASK BEFORE REMOVING — T.)

items.prompt: 11:40. Twenty minutes to the noon news. What's the last thing you do?
items.happening: Stream in sync, measured at the viewer's end.
unknown: When the next update will change latency
items.risk: The next careful person — and the next update.
timeout: The noon news starts. The setting is right and unlabeled.
Fixed isn't finished until the reason is written where the next person looks.

options.label: Label the setting with its reason, add a weekly viewer-end sync check, tell the newsroom it's fixed and why
options.result: Tess prints the label herself: 167 ms = STREAM VIDEO PROCESSING · ASK BEFORE REMOVING.
options.consequence: The next careful person reads the reason instead of guessing.

options.label: Nothing — it's in sync now
options.result: It stays in sync until the next encoder update changes the latency.
options.fail: The same trap is still set.

options.label: Lock the setting so nobody can change it
options.result: Next month an update changes the video latency and nobody can compensate.
options.consequence: A lock without a reason is just a slower trap.
options.fail: Settings must change when the chain changes — with the reason in view.

options.label: Ask Omar to check his own lips on the app every morning
options.result: Omar: “I'm an anchor, not a test pattern.”
options.consequence: A person as a monitoring system.

items.alt: The noon news, live: Omar at the anchor desk, the studio clock at twelve exactly, the lower third reading Kestrel Valley News, Noon.
items.caption: 12:00:00. On Dolores's phone, the word and the lips arrive together for the first time since Tuesday.

items.alt: Omar stops by Tess's desk in the newsroom.

bubbles.text: In twenty years I've been late for plenty. You're the first person who ever made me early.

items.alt: Cal's fourteen warnings on the wall. Number six — lip-sync never checked at the viewer — is crossed out in red. Tess points at it.
items.caption: Warning #6: crossed off. Thirteen to go.

items.alt: Cal's empty chair at the master-control desk. His headset hangs on its hook. A mug marked C. sits where he left it.
narration: Nobody has moved Cal's mug. Nobody has said his name all day. The coffee in it has grown a skin.
items.caption: The building keeps his shape.

items.alt: Vera, the news director, silver hair, reading glasses pushed up, reads a complaints summary on a screen: ads too loud, thirty-one times.

bubbles.text: Why are the ads SO much louder than the news? Thirty-one people want to know. So do I.

items.caption: Next: *Too Loud.*

lines.text: I want a number by four. A number, not a feeling.
A number, or the right number?
Thirty years in news. If you're good, those are the same thing. Also — the loudest spot is Ivo's. Ivo is my best producer. Be careful.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  Measure lip sync where viewers watch, with a flash and a beep. Compare paths: what differs is where the cause lives. Compensate by a measured number, re-measure, and label the reason next to the setting. When someone careful removed it, the label failed first.

REFLECTION (optional)  · Tess wrote down why she removed the delay. Nobody had written down why it was there. Which setting in your world has no reason next to it?  Boundary: this reflection doesn't change any setting.
